documents: Fang, Geng & Xiu (2022), Typhoon Effects on the Vertical Chlorophyll Distribution on the Northern Shelf of the South China Sea, JGR Oceans 127, e2022JC019350 (published PDF, 18 pp.; no supplement, review file, or earlier version supplied)

entry.evidence: However, the vertical distribution of phytoplankton in response to the combined influences of typhoons, upwelling, and river discharge still remains unclear.

steps.action: Pose the open question of how the vertical phytoplankton (Chla) distribution responds to the combined influences of typhoons, upwelling and river discharge on the northern SCS shelf.
steps.quote: the vertical distribution of phytoplankton in response to the combined influences of typhoons, upwelling, and river discharge still remains unclear

steps.action: Take from other groups' work the candidate drivers of typhoon-induced Chla change: vertical mixing offshore, increased Pearl River discharge nearshore, and upwelling.
steps.quote: phytoplankton biomass and primary production increased dramatically offshore after Typhoon Koppu due to vertical mixing

steps.action: Use the live passage of Typhoon Merbok (June 2017) to sample transect S1 with CTD and fluorescence before and after the storm, adding 2008 and 2018 cruises along S1 for comparison.
steps.quote: two cruises were conducted before and after Typhoon Merbok's passage

steps.action: Build a coupled ROMS (1/24°, Mellor-Yamada closure) and modified CoSiNE biogeochemical model with photoacclimation, run with real-time forcing for 2016-2018.
steps.quote: A coupled physical-biogeochemical model was constructed in this study.

steps.action: Design two model experiments besides the control: NoRiver (river turned off from 1 January 2017) and ZMix (advection terms turned off on 10 June 2017) to separate driver contributions.
steps.quote: two experiments (NoRiver and ZMix) were conducted to examine the influence of the Pearl River on and the roles of advection and vertical mixing

steps.action: Describe satellite wind and SST (cold wake right of track, shift to upwelling-favorable southwesterlies) and in situ surface and S1-section T, S and Chla before and after the typhoon: BCM/SCM weakened, shoaled nearshore and deepened offshore.
steps.quote: The BCM/SCM concentration decreased and the SCM layer became relatively diffuse in the water column after the typhoon

steps.action: Validate the model against satellite and in situ data (correlations 0.93 for temperature, 0.95 salinity, 0.6 Chla), against observed pre-post differences along S1, and against the GHRSST cold wake, noting surface discrepancies from plume misplacement.
steps.quote: For all the transects, the correlation coefficient between the modeled and observed temperatures was 0.93

steps.action: Correlate the normalized SCM depth (NSD) with the normalized depth of the 25 °C isotherm (NDD) across all 2008, 2017 and 2018 measurements.
steps.quote: We found that the NSD was correlated with the NDD (r = 0.83, p < 0.01

steps.action: Set the NSD-NDD link against the published finding that upwelling shoals the SCM toward the coast.
steps.quote: This result is consistent with that of Lu et al. (2010), which showed that the SCM shoals toward the coast as a result of upwelling.

steps.action: From the pre-post NSD/NDD changes, propose upwelling for nearshore shoaling and vertical mixing for offshore deepening, and add seawater/plume movement and river discharge as further candidate causes of the Chla change.
steps.quote: It is noteworthy that typhoon-induced vertical mixing may not be the only reason for the Chla change.

steps.action: Use gauged Pearl River discharge at three stations to exclude increased river discharge as the cause of the immediate Chla change, since discharge rose only after 16 June.
steps.quote: the discharges measured at the three major river stations (Boluo, Shijiao, Gaoyao) of the Pearl River did not change immediately after the typhoon

steps.action: Decompose the modeled Chla tendency into horizontal and vertical advection, vertical diffusion and biological terms on an averaged A1-box cross section, neglecting horizontal diffusion.
steps.quote: The dynamics of Chla change in response to the typhoon were further examined through phytoplankton Chla budget analysis in the CTL run of the model

steps.action: Compare velocities, vertical viscosity and RATE among CTL, NoRiver and ZMix runs to attribute surface Chla change to plume retreat, upper-layer gain and SCM loss to mixing, and BCM shoaling to continued upwelling.
steps.quote: suggesting that the onshore movement or retreat of plume water was the dominant factor contributing to the change in surface Chla

steps.action: Check that the model reproduces the published contrast of high N/P in the plume and low N/P in the upwelling region.
steps.quote: The model can reproduce this feature (Figure 11c).

steps.action: Infer nutrient redistribution (PO4 rise in plume, NO3 and PO4 rise in bottom intrusion water) and the time series of budget terms in nearshore and offshore A1 boxes, finding biological production rising after 13 June, more strongly nearshore.
steps.quote: The RB was positive and increased gradually in the BCM layer after 13 June, which dominated the RATE change.

steps.action: Set the model attribution against previous typhoon studies on the shelf: consistent offshore (advection and mixing), qualifying the river-discharge explanation nearshore.
steps.quote: the Chla change was attributed to advection and vertical mixing, which was consistent with the findings of previous studies

steps.action: Keep the claim that the immediate Chla change was physically driven and the later change was biological plus physical, strongest in the subsurface and nearshore.
steps.quote: the subsequent gradual change in Chla was due to both biological and physical processes, particularly in the subsurface layer

tree.answer: Yes: BCM/SCM weakened, shoaled nearshore and deepened offshore after Typhoon Merbok
Chla change observed directly by CTD fluorescence; driving processes not observed, inferred with a coupled model
Explain the mechanism of the vertical Chla change (attribution of drivers)
Vertical mixing, upwelling/advection, plume movement, river discharge, biological production
Partly: ablation runs (NoRiver, ZMix) and budget terms separate the drivers' contributions
Conditions found in a live event (one typhoon, two cruises)

tree.question: 6b
tree.answer: Partly: 2008 and 2018 cruises repeat the NSD-NDD relation, not the typhoon response
Model validated against observations; no parameter sensitivity tests or second typhoon
Physical processes dominate immediate change, biology plus physics later; best explanation

end.claim: During and after Typhoon Merbok the immediate Chla change on the northern SCS shelf was caused mainly by physical processes (plume movement, vertical mixing, upwelling), and the subsequent gradual change by both biological and physical processes, especially in the subsurface layer and more strongly nearshore.

decisive_move.sentence: Without comparing the control run with the NoRiver and ZMix runs (and the budget terms), the observed Chla change could not be attributed to plume movement, mixing, upwelling or biology.

gates.evidence: The cruises were run to investigate the typhoon's impact, not to test a stated hypothesis (p. 2). The model faced validation against observations it could have failed (pp. 7-8), and the river-discharge cause could have failed against gauge data (p. 10), but the attribution itself rests on model ablations without an independent test. Nothing is reported as fixed before the data.

imports.item: Natural neighbor interpolation of station data to maps
Geider et al. (1997) photoacclimation model with variable chlorophyll-to-biomass ratio

limits: No review file, supplement or earlier version was supplied; supplementary validation figures (S1-S8) are cited but not seen. The coding is from the published text only. Composition is none_fits: conditions are found in a single live event (one typhoon), observed once before and once after, and mechanisms are attributed by model ablation runs and a budget analysis; this is not a trace series over independent traces, and there is no crucial test among rivals. Sub-claims at other statuses: the observed BCM/SCM weakening, shoaling nearshore and deepening offshore is a direct observation from two CTD sections; the NSD-NDD relation (r = 0.83) is a regularity_in_range across 2008, 2017 and 2018 cruises; the delayed river discharge (after 16 June) is an observation that excludes discharge as the immediate cause. The paper reports no parameter sensitivity tests, no uncertainty on budget terms, no fluorescence-to-Chla calibration, and no second typhoon. Model Chla skill is modest (R = 0.6), with surface discrepancies attributed (as the authors infer) to misplacement of the plume. Whether the ablation runs were planned before the cruise data were seen is not stated (inference: they were designed after).

disagreements.target: Previous studies identifying typhoon-enhanced river discharge as a key nearshore factor (Liu et al., 2013; Zhao et al., 2009)
disagreements.support: Gauge data show Pearl River discharge rose only about a week after Merbok, and the model attributes the change within a few days to plume extent and up/downwelling instead.
disagreements.quote: For Typhoon Merbok, we showed that the Pearl River discharge increased approximately 1 week after the typhoon

disagreements.target: Previous studies on typhoon-induced mixing transporting phytoplankton upward (Chacko, 2017)
disagreements.support: The authors argue that seawater and plume movement and river input also contribute, and the model runs show plume retreat dominating the nearshore surface change.
disagreements.quote: It is noteworthy that typhoon-induced vertical mixing may not be the only reason for the Chla change.

alternatives_considered.chosen: Chla budget without the horizontal diffusion term
alternatives_considered.reason: its magnitude is much smaller than those of the other terms
